inputs.need:
I am a GP and the clinical director of a primary care network of seven practices. We employ four social prescribing link workers, who took about 1,600 referrals last year for people with loneliness, low mood, debt and housing worries, long-term conditions and frequent attendance. The integrated care board is deciding whether to fund more link workers across the area, and its commissioning board has asked networks for a clear account of what the evidence says, because the published picture is confusing. Some reviews conclude that social prescribing improves wellbeing and reduces GP appointments; others say the studies are too weak to conclude anything, and the same handful of small evaluations seems to be counted again and again.

We want to do an umbrella review: find the existing reviews of link worker social prescribing, judge their quality, work out how much they overlap, and summarise what they show for wellbeing, loneliness, GP consultation rates and costs, and for whom. I especially want to know whether people with the most complex needs benefit, because those are the people our link workers spend most time with.

I have two protected sessions a week until February, and our network analyst can help with data management. There is no funding. We cannot collect new data from patients for this piece of work; it has to rest on what has already been published. The report goes to the commissioning board at the end of February 2027, and I would rather tell them honestly that the evidence is uncertain than oversell it.

records.title: Social prescribing through link workers and patient wellbeing: a systematic review
records.abstract: We searched six databases to 2018 for evaluations of social prescribing delivered through a link worker. Fourteen studies were included, most of them uncontrolled before-after evaluations of local schemes. Eleven reported improved wellbeing scores after referral, but only two had a comparison group and neither found a clear difference. Attrition between referral and follow-up exceeded 40 percent in half the studies. We judged the evidence insufficient to show that link worker social prescribing improves wellbeing, and we call for controlled evaluations with complete follow-up.

records.title: Link worker social prescribing and primary care consultation rates: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Achterberg-Nkemelu J, Sorensen-Pike A, Dasgupta-Rowe M
records.abstract: We included nine controlled studies of link worker social prescribing that reported primary care consultations. Pooled across seven studies, consultation rates at 12 months were 15 percent lower after referral than in comparison groups (rate ratio 0.85, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.98), with substantial heterogeneity. Comparison groups were usually patients who were not referred, and only one study was randomised. Effects were larger in studies of frequent attenders, where regression to the mean is likely. We rate the certainty of evidence as low.

records.title: Effects of social prescribing on loneliness: a systematic review of controlled studies
records.authors: Kowalski-Asante B, Lindgren-Oyelaran P, Moreau-Tanaka E
records.venue: Journal of Loneliness and Social Health
records.abstract: We identified seven controlled studies of social prescribing that measured loneliness, including two randomised trials. The pooled effect on loneliness was small and uncertain (standardised mean difference -0.08, 95 percent CI -0.21 to 0.05). Participants valued the relationship with the link worker, but the activities they were referred to were often unavailable or too far away. Studies rarely reported how many referrals led to sustained participation in community activities. Certainty was low because of imprecision and risk of bias, and follow-up rarely extended beyond six months.

records.title: Economic evaluations of social prescribing: a systematic review
records.abstract: We reviewed six economic evaluations of social prescribing schemes. Four reported savings from fewer GP and emergency department attendances, but all used before-after comparisons without a control group, and savings disappeared in the one analysis that adjusted for regression to the mean. Costs of the voluntary sector activities that patients were referred to were rarely counted. We conclude that claims of net savings are not supported by robust evidence and that future evaluations should include community sector costs and a comparison group.

records.title: Who is referred to social prescribing and who benefits? A realist review
records.abstract: Drawing on 48 documents, we developed programme theories for how link worker social prescribing works. Benefits depended on link workers having enough time to build trust, on available and affordable community activities, and on the person's readiness to engage. People with complex needs, such as debt, insecure housing and severe mental illness, often needed many more contacts and were more likely to disengage when referred onward too quickly. The review cannot estimate effect sizes but explains why averages may hide very different outcomes for different groups.

records.title: Overlap of primary studies across systematic reviews of social prescribing: a citation matrix analysis
records.abstract: We built a citation matrix of the primary studies included in 11 systematic reviews of social prescribing published between 2017 and 2023. The reviews included 97 unique primary studies, and the corrected covered area was 18 percent, indicating very high overlap. Six small uncontrolled evaluations were included in eight or more reviews. Reviews reaching positive conclusions leaned more heavily on these evaluations than reviews reaching uncertain conclusions. We recommend that overviews count each primary study once and report conclusions against a citation matrix.

records.title: Social prescribing: an overview of systematic reviews
records.abstract: We searched for systematic reviews of social prescribing to March 2017 and found five, all of low or critically low quality. The reviews agreed that participants reported feeling better but disagreed on effects on service use. None of the reviews assessed overlap between their included studies, and none separated link worker models from direct referral by clinicians. We conclude that the evidence was insufficient to support or reject investment and recommend an updated overview once controlled studies are published, with an assessment of overlap.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Reviews of link worker social prescribing report better wellbeing mainly from uncontrolled evaluations, a 15 percent lower consultation rate from non-randomised comparisons, and no clear effect on loneliness. Claimed savings do not survive adjustment for regression to the mean. Reviews overlap heavily, and positive conclusions lean on the same small evaluations. A realist review explains why people with complex needs may benefit less. The one earlier overview is out of date.

response.overview: Umbrella review of systematic reviews of link worker social prescribing published from 2017, with quality appraisal of each review, a citation matrix of primary studies and separate certainty ratings per outcome.
response.population: Systematic reviews (including realist and economic reviews) of social prescribing delivered through a link worker to adults, published January 2017 to December 2026.
response.exposure: Link worker social prescribing compared with usual care or no referral, as defined by each review; direct clinician referral schemes are excluded unless reported separately.
response.procedures: The GP searches four databases and two review registers with a dated strategy; the analyst manages records. Two readers (the GP and a second clinician for a random 30 percent) screen and appraise reviews with AMSTAR 2. A citation matrix lists every primary study against every review; the corrected covered area is calculated overall and per outcome. For each outcome, conclusions are summarised from the highest-quality, most recent review with the least overlap, and certainty is graded with GRADE.

response.title: Link worker social prescribing: an umbrella review of wellbeing, loneliness, consultation and cost outcomes with an overlap analysis
response.abstract: Objective: to summarise what systematic reviews show about link worker social prescribing once review quality and overlap are taken into account. Design: umbrella review of reviews published from 2017, with AMSTAR 2 appraisal, a citation matrix and GRADE per outcome. Results and conclusions will be written after the synthesis.
response.introduction: Reviews of social prescribing reach conflicting conclusions and draw heavily on the same small evaluations. Commissioners need an account that counts each primary study once.
response.methods: Four databases and two registers were searched for reviews from January 2017. Reviews were appraised with AMSTAR 2; a citation matrix and the corrected covered area measured overlap; each outcome was graded separately.
response.results: No reviews have been screened yet. The report will present the review flow, appraisal, the citation matrix, and outcome-level findings with certainty.
response.discussion: The discussion will explain disagreements between reviews through overlap and study design and set out what the evidence supports for funding decisions.
response.limitations: Dependence on existing reviews, a single main reviewer, and published data only.
response.conclusion: To be written after the synthesis.
